relations.note: Ukko sends iron hail against Hiisi’s fiery horse and opposes harmful beings with celestial weapons.
After Louhi conceals the luminaries, Ukko’s celestial fire aids attempts to restore light.
Louhi asks Ukko to destroy Kalevala, but his consent is not stated.

relations.myth: Hunt for the Elk of Hiisi
relations.note: She shares forest authority, carrying keys and opening Tapio’s storehouse of game.
Mielikki is Tapio’s wife and co-ruler, holding keys to his game-storehouse.
Tapio can designate the female forest divinity or forest itself, overlapping Mielikki’s identity.
Mielikki raises the bear, which Tapio later yields to the hunters.

Akka.note: Later pantheon-builders made Akka Ukko’s wife from paired common nouns and Sámi comparisons.

Annikki.note: Annikki appears beside Mielikki as they control forest dogs and the bear.

Christian God.note: Ukko’s titles and Jumala formulas overlap under Christian influence, sometimes approaching monotheistic language.

Daughter of the Air.note: The air maiden casts material from heaven, after which Mielikki gathers and nurtures the bear.

Elk of Hiisi.myth: Construction of the Elk of Hiisi
Elk of Hiisi.note: Hiisi and his folk construct and animate an elk from forest materials.

Elk of Hiisi.myth: Hunt for the Elk of Hiisi
Elk of Hiisi.note: Mielikki is petitioned to open the forest storehouse and release the supernatural elk toward the hunter.

Hiiden väki.myth: Construction of the Elk of Hiisi
Hiiden väki.note: Hiisi directs his folk as they construct the supernatural elk.

Hiisi’s horse.note: Hiisi possesses the dangerous supernatural horse sought in Lemminkäinen’s bridal task.

Ilmarinen.note: Louhi requires Ilmarinen to forge the Sampo before courting her daughter.
Louhi imposes supernatural tasks and accepts Ilmarinen after he completes them.
Louhi conducts the wedding after Ilmarinen wins her daughter.
After his wife's death, Ilmarinen requests another daughter, but Louhi refuses.
Ilmarinen joins the expedition that removes Louhi's Sampo from Pohjola.

Ilmarinen.myth: Release of the sun and moon
Ilmarinen.note: Louhi releases the lights after Ilmarinen begins forging tools to liberate them.
Ilmarinen invokes Ukko to provide snow and cool destructive fire.

Ilmarinen.myth: Origins of iron and celestial fire
Ilmarinen.note: Regional variants redistribute atmospheric, smithing, iron, and fire-making functions between Ukko and Ilmarinen.

Ilmatar.note: Ilmatar appeals to Ukko for release from pregnancy, but he does not answer directly.

Juutas/Jutas.note: Later poetry and dictionaries use this Judas-derived name parallel to Hiisi.

Lemminkäinen.note: Louhi assigns three supernatural tasks that Lemminkäinen must complete for her daughter.
Louhi excludes him from the wedding and later summons Pohjola's people against him.
Ukko answers Lemminkäinen by opening heaven and sending iron hail against the fiery horse.

Lempo.note: Charms and the Kalevala use Lempo and Hiisi as parallel hostile substitutes.

Loviatar.note: Louhi assists as midwife or recipient when Loviatar bears nine afflictions.

Nyyrikki.myth: Hunt for the Elk of Hiisi
Nyyrikki.note: Nyyrikki clears the hunter’s road while Mielikki is petitioned to release game.
Later systematization presents Nyyrikki as the son of Tapio and Mielikki.
Nyyrikki is explicitly called Tapio’s son.

Nyyrikki.myth: Hunt for the Elk of Hiisi
Nyyrikki.note: Tapio is invoked while Nyyrikki marks the route to the elk.
Tapio’s son lays tree bridges and guides cattle safely across marshland.

Näkki.note: One South Karelian tradition makes Näkki the offspring of Ahti and Vellamo.

Otso.note: Louhi calls or sends Otso to kill Kalevala's livestock.
Some bear-origin variants make Mielikki the bear’s mother or progenitress.

Otso.myth: Mielikki raises Ohto beneath a spruce
Otso.note: Mielikki fosters and raises the bear beneath the flowering crown of a spruce.

Otso.myth: The bear receives claws and teeth
Otso.note: Mielikki provides the bear claws and teeth after it swears against using them wickedly.
Mielikki restrains the bear, binding its muzzle or dulling its claws near cattle.
Tapio yields his cherished forest animal and joins his household at its feast.

Pakkanen.note: Frost freezes Ahti at sea, though Ahti may denote the sea or hero.

Rauni.note: Agricola calls Rauni “Ukko’s woman”; her action precedes Ukko’s powerful thundering.

Saint Anne.note: Saint Anne enters forest poetry as Annikki, functioning as a counterpart or substitute for forest women.

Snake.note: Hiisi’s foam or saliva forms the snake, which he sometimes animates.

Syöjätär.note: Syöjätär consumes or expels Hiisi’s foam, helping form the snake.

Sämpsä Pellervöinen.note: Ahti and Sämpsä occupy parallel poetic slots as ploughmen without necessarily meeting.

Tavaj.note: Krohn and Harva compared or equated Tapio with this Kola Sámi being.

Tellervo.note: Tellervo occupies overlapping wife, daughter, maiden, and attendant roles within Mielikki’s forest household.
Tellervo appears as Tapio’s maiden or daughter.
Tellervo protects cattle in Tapio’s forest domain.
One formula calls Tellervo Tapio’s wife, conflicting with her maiden status.
The same runo also calls Tellervo Tapio’s maiden, preserving conflicting formulas.

Three maidens of iron.note: Ukko produces three maidens from his hands and knee; their milk becomes forms of iron.

Tuometar.note: Tuometar shares with Mielikki the task of controlling or restraining the bear.
Tuometar is named Tapio’s daughter in a cattle-protection charm.

Tuulikki.myth: Hunt for the Elk of Hiisi
Tuulikki.note: Tuulikki drives the elk while Mielikki opens the forest storehouse and releases game.

Tyytikki.note: Tyytikki shares animal-driving or bear-restraining duties with Mielikki in variant forest poetry.

Vellamo.note: Later folklore and scholarship describe Vellamo as Ahti’s wife and complementary female water-ruler.
They are jointly invoked as complementary rulers of water and fish.
Both emerge from the water and listen separately to Väinämöinen’s music.

Virgin Mary.myth: Heavenly descent and nurture of the bear
Virgin Mary.note: Mary sends or handles the bear’s heavenly material before Mielikki nurtures it in the forest.
Mary can replace Mielikki or related female forest guardians in bear and cattle-protection charms.

Väinämöinen.note: Ahto rises onto a water lily, listens, and praises Väinämöinen’s kantele playing.
Väinämöinen invokes Ahto and asks him to drive fish toward the net.
Louhi receives and treats the stranded hero before bargaining for his return.
Louhi demands a Sampo as the price for returning Väinämöinen home.
Louhi hosts Väinämöinen while her daughter conditions or refuses his courtship.
Väinämöinen leads the heroes who seize Louhi's Sampo from Pohjola.
Louhi pursues Väinämöinen, transforms into a great bird, and fights him.
Louhi sends illnesses against Kalevala, and Väinämöinen heals the afflicted people.
Louhi sends a bear against the cattle, but Väinämöinen kills it.
Louhi's deeds cause darkness while Väinämöinen pursues and recovers the celestial spark.

Väinämöinen.myth: Release of the sun and moon
Väinämöinen.note: Väinämöinen fails to open the rock; Louhi later releases the imprisoned lights.
Väinämöinen invokes Mielikki before hunting the bear and recounts her nurturing of it.
Väinämöinen invokes Ukko for rain, healing, protection, weather, and help completing tasks.

calamities.note: Louhi is described as the mother and controller of calamities.

north wind.note: Lencqvist conjectures that Louhi is the wife of the north wind.

the nine diseases.note: Later synthesis identifies Louhi herself as mother of nine diseases.
Louhi dispatches the personified diseases against the people of Kalevala.
